summary: BBN's report on ARPANET host status for January 3 to 15, 1972. It was replaced by RFC 298.

eli5.summary: A status check on which network computers answered during two weeks in January.

subtitle: BBN's status report on ARPANET host availability for January 1972.

tldr.problem: ARPANET sites needed to know which hosts were available and reliable for network access on a regular basis.
tldr.mechanism: BBN continued its practice of testing and reporting host status every two weeks, gathering information from site contacts and daily automated login attempts from their Terminal IMP.
tldr.outcome: This report covered January 3-15, 1972, showing which hosts were servers and which were user-only or under development, helping the network community understand availability patterns. RFC 293 also updated RFC 288 with a corrected host status table.

today: RFC 293 was replaced by RFC 298 as operational monitoring continued. This report exemplifies the challenges of early ARPANET management: unreliable communication links and heterogeneous host computers made achieving consistent availability difficult.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 293 reports on the status of most ARPANET hosts from January 3 to January 15, 1972. Ellen Westheimer at BBN continued the biweekly reporting practice established in RFC 235, gathering status information from site operators and conducting daily automated tests.

The testing captured a snapshot of network availability in early 1972, when the ARPANET had about 15 operational sites and many hosts were still under development or transitioning to new hardware.
sections.eli5: BBN checked every few days to see which computers were working and ready for visitors on the network during these two weeks in January.

sections.title: Host Categories and Status Codes
sections.content:
Hosts fell into several categories. Some were not expected to be network servers for at least two weeks (like CASE and Ames), and therefore were not included in daily testing. Others were user-only sites or Terminal IMPs (like the Network Control Center at address 5).

The RFC uses status codes for each login test: O for open and accessible, D for dead or inaccessible, T for timed out, H for half-open (connected but then closed), and R for refused. The tables show daily test results across the period.
sections.eli5: Some computers weren't being tested because they weren't ready yet. For those that were tested, the codes showed: O for working, D for dead, T for too slow, H for half-working, and R for refusing the connection.

sections.title: Status Data
sections.content:
The RFC includes tables showing which computers were servers, user-only, or under development, plus daily test results from nine different dates spanning January 3-15. The data reveals the unreliability of early networking: hosts frequently timed out, became inaccessible, or only half-opened connections.

Notably, UCLA's SIGMA-7 and IBM-360/91, SRI's NIC PDP-10, and BBN's PDP-10 showed relatively good availability, while others like Stanford's PDP-10 and Case's PDP-10 had poor connectivity during this period.
sections.eli5: The tables show which computers worked on different days. Some were reliable, but many would stop answering calls from time to time.

references.text: McKenzie, A., et al., "ARPA Network Handbook", RFC 288, December 1971.
